claim: To revoke an active permission set session, AWS's procedure adds the user's ID to a Deny policy in an SCP and keeps it in place for at least 12 hours; otherwise a user with an active IAM role session gets the role's actions back, and after 12 hours the active sessions expire.
question: How long must the Deny policy stay in place when revoking an IAM Identity Center user's active role sessions, and why?

values.display: will have restored actions with the IAM role

qualifiers.condition: a deny policy for the user in an SCP

evidence.quote: If you wait 12 hours, active sessions expire and the user will not be able to access the IAM role again.
Otherwise, the user with an active IAM role session will have restored actions with the IAM role.
We assume that the deny all policy is present in a service control policy (SCP).

claim: If a user has an active AWS access portal session and is disabled, the user can continue to assume new roles until their permission set assignments are removed; deleting the user's active session makes the user lose access to the AWS access portal immediately.
question: Is disabling an IAM Identity Center user enough to stop them from assuming roles at once?

values.display: they can continue to assume new roles
immediately lose access to the AWS access portal

qualifiers.scope: revoking IAM Identity Center user access
qualifiers.condition: the user has an active AWS access portal session

evidence.quote: If a user has an active AWS access portal session and you disable the user, they can continue to assume new roles until you remove their access.
After deleting a user session, the user will immediately lose access to the AWS access portal.

claim: Temporary elevated access (just-in-time access) is a way to request, approve and track the use of a permission for a specific task during a specified time; IAM Identity Center provides it by integrating with solutions from AWS Security Competency partners.
question: Is just-in-time (temporary elevated) access built into IAM Identity Center or provided by partners?

values.display: solutions from AWS Security Competency partners

qualifiers.scope: temporary elevated access with IAM Identity Center

evidence.quote: Temporary elevated access (also known as just-in-time access) is a way to request, approve, and track the use of a permission to perform a specific task during a specified time.
To address a range of customers' needs, AWS IAM Identity Center integrates with the solutions from AWS Security Competency partners.

claim: Users of the connected directory can be given permissions to the management account or member accounts based on common job functions or custom permissions, and IAM Identity Center configures all the necessary user permissions in the AWS accounts automatically.
question: Who creates the IAM permissions in each AWS account when IAM Identity Center assigns access?

values.display: configures all the necessary user permissions

qualifiers.scope: single sign-on access to AWS accounts

evidence.quote: Or you can use custom permissions to meet your specific security requirements.
IAM Identity Center configures all the necessary user permissions in your AWS accounts automatically.

claim: Trusted identity propagation adds identity context to an IAM role to identify the user requesting access, propagates it to other AWS services so their administrators can grant permissions based on user attributes such as group associations, and lets them audit who accessed what data in service logs or CloudTrail.
question: What is trusted identity propagation?

values.display: identity context is added to an IAM role
user attributes such as group associations

evidence.quote: Trusted identity propagation is a feature of IAM Identity Center that enables administrators of AWS services to grant permissions based on user attributes such as group associations. With trusted identity propagation, identity context is added to an IAM role to identify the user requesting access to AWS resources. This context is propagated to other AWS services.
In addition, they can audit who accessed what data by looking at service logs or AWS CloudTrail.

claim: By default, assignments are required for AWS managed applications, so only users assigned to the application directly or through a group see its tile in the AWS access portal; an application administrator can choose not to require assignments.
question: Can every IAM Identity Center user open an AWS managed application by default?

values.display: assignments are required for AWS managed applications

qualifiers.condition: the application administrator can choose whether to require assignments

evidence.quote: By default, assignments are required for AWS managed applications. If you are an application administrator, you can choose whether to require assignments to an application.
If assignments are required, when users sign in to the AWS access portal, only users who are assigned to the application directly or through a group assignment can view the application tile.
